nodes.statement: The minimum network width N_c(w) required to achieve zero violation on w constraints grows sublinearly with w for standard feedforward networks, indicating solution space rigidity emerges from architectural inductive biases rather than constraint density.

When constraints form a linear manifold in input space, N_c(w) remains bounded as w increases, supporting solution space rigidity; when constraints are nonlinearly distributed, N_c(w) grows linearly or superlinearly, indicating a fat solution space.

The presence of sharp minima in the loss landscape correlates with higher N_c(w) values, suggesting that optimization-induced bias toward flat minima effectively reduces solution space dimensionality, making the effective space appear more rigid than the theoretical space.

The solution space for constraint-satisfying neural networks can be characterized by a variational principle where minimizing constraint violation energy corresponds to finding the minimum norm solution; N_c(w) remains bounded if the constraint energy functional is coercive, indicating rigidity.

In the infinite-width limit, neural networks satisfy a PDE (Neural Tangent Kernel equation); if this PDE is elliptic, the solution space is rigid (N_c(w) bounded), while hyperbolic character indicates a fat space (N_c(w) grows with w).

The solution space of the constraint system exhibits topological rigidity (vanishing first homology), meaning that as w increases, the feasible manifold does not branch into disconnected components, thereby allowing small-width networks to generalize without increasing N_c.
